Off the coast of Antarctica, the sea star Odontaster validus exhibits a remarkably slow pace of life, finely tuned to the frigid conditions of the Southern Ocean. In laboratory aquaria maintained at a constant water temperature of -1.5 °C [T = -1.5 °C], newly hatched juveniles emerge from the egg capsule after an incubation period of 33 days [ab = 33 days]. At this stage, the chord length at birth is a mere 0.042 cm [Lb = 0.042 cm], a measure of the straight-line distance from the anterior to the posterior of the tiny larva. This diminutive size underscores the substantial energetic constraints imposed by the cold environment. The developmental trajectory from birth to the completion of metamorphosis, a process involving a radical reorganisation of the body plan from a bilateral larva to a rudimentary juvenile sea star, requires an additional period of 132 days  under the same thermal regime at a temperature of -1.5 °C [T = -1.5 °C]. Cold temperatures are known to slow enzymatic reaction rates, thus prolonging developmental stages, and these observed durations are consistent with the general pattern seen in other polar echinoderms.

Following the larval-juvenile transition, the post-metamorphic juveniles of Odontaster validus gradually increase in size and mass. Upon completion of metamorphosis, the arm length at metam, which is measured from the central mouth to the tip of a single arm and averaged across three arms, is approximately 0.14 cm . This marks the beginning of a lengthy sub-adult phase during which the juvenile must forage on the seabed for diatoms and detritus to fuel its growth. The juveniles eventually reach puberty, defined here as the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive maturity. This critical developmental milestone is associated with an arm length st puberty of 2 cm [Lp = 2 cm] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 2.95 grams [Wwp = 2.95 grams]. Reaching these morphological thresholds appears to be a prerequisite for the activation of the gonad, as individuals smaller than this size typically lack differentiated gonadal tissue. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active adults is 10% [GSI = 10%] at a stable temperature of -1.5 °C [T = -1.5 °C].

The reproductive strategy of Odontaster validus is characterised by a relatively low investment per offspring but a potentially protracted breeding period. The egg dry weight of an individual ovum is approximately 1.1 micrograms , placing this species among the echinoderms with small, planktotrophic eggs that produce feeding larvae. For a female to achieve this output, she must divert a portion of the energy acquired from feeding on sponges and microbial films into oocyte production. The ultimate arm length for a fully grown adult, again measured as the average radius from the mouth to the arm tip, reaches about 7 cm [Li = about 7 cm]. This asymptotic size is a key determinant of an individual's feeding radius and its ability to access prey items. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a large, reproductively active adult can reach 100 grams [Wwi = 100 grams], though this value is rarely attained by individuals in the most food-limited microhabitats. The data on size and reproduction suggest that O. validus prioritises slow, steady somatic growth over rapid mass accumulation.

Long-term field studies and captive observations have allowed researchers to estimate the lifespan of Odontaster validus with some confidence. Based on mark-recapture data and analysis of growth lines in the ossicles, the oldest documented individuals in a stable environment maintained at -1.5 °C [T = -1.5 °C] have a life span of approximately 14,600 days [am = approximately 14,600 days], which converts to roughly 40 years. This extraordinary longevity, rivaling that of many deep-sea and polar invertebrates, is a direct consequence of the extreme cold and the associated reduction in metabolic maintenance costs. A starfish that lives for four decades must contend with slow predation pressure from ribbon worms and other sea stars but also faces the cumulative risk of physical damage from anchor ice and shifting brash ice. The ability to persist for this duration allows for repeated spawning events over many years, which is a classic bet-hedging strategy in unpredictable environments. Reproduction frequency, however, is thought to be biennial or triennial for many females due to the lengthy vitellogenic cycle required to mature a new batch of oocytes.

Comparisons with related species from temperate and tropical waters highlight the extreme life-history strategies employed by Odontaster validus. Where a tropical sea star might grow from a 0.042 cm [Lb = 0.042 cm] juvenile to a sexually mature adult with an arm length st puberty of 2 cm [Lp = 2 cm] in a matter of months, the same ontogenetic transition in O. validus takes many years. The metabolic constraint imposed by the constant temperature of -1.5 °C [T = -1.5 °C] essentially serves as a physiological brake on development. The gonadosomatic index was 10% [GSI = 10%] at a temperature of -1.5 °C [T = -1.5 °C]. An individual that reaches the ultimate wet weight of 100 grams [Wwi = 100 grams] may invest a relatively small fraction of that mass into eggs, reflecting the fundamental energetic trade-off between maintaining a large body size for feeding and mobility and producing the next generation. This finely balanced life history is a testament to the species' successful adaptation to one of the most demanding environments on Earth.
